Read tool use as design work

Name language, medium, and support. Then trace prompts, edits, and refusals — not only the final surface.

Image: Operator at a mid-century card-punching machine.

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

1 · Stage the tool

Use generative tools for early variation; keep problem framing and final judgment human.

Image: Room of punched-card machines at Bletchley Park, 1945.

Bletchley Park 1945 photo of punched card machines · Jack Good; Donald Michie; Geoffrey Timms · Public domain · Source

  • Early variation is not the same as outsourcing the brief.
  • Name the stage before you open a tool.
  • Final form and responsibility stay with the designer.

Source: course wording from unit enrichment (Park / studio pedagogy still pending page-level citation resolve).

Ask: Where in your last brief did a tool belong — and where did it not?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

2 · Show the process

Prompts, selection decisions, and re-authoring belong in the portfolio — not only the polished output.

Screen-glow winter. A thousand options. No taste. Who closed the door?

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Technicians reprogramming ENIAC by replugging cables.

Reprogramming ENIAC · U.S. Army · Public domain · Source

  • Process transparency is a design ethic, not a software feature.
  • Record what you asked, what you kept, and what you rejected.
  • Assessment should be able to read your judgment, not only your render.

Source: course wording; fieldlex process transparency.

Ask: What would a critic miss if they saw only your final file?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

3 · Refuse originality theatre

Fast, pretty outputs without problem framing are empty craft — they perform novelty without a brief.

Image: UNIVAC file computer installation photograph.

UNIVAC-FILE-COMPUTER-BRL61-0944 · U.S. Army Ballistic Research Laboratory · Public domain · Source

  • High speed can hide weak framing.
  • Originality theatre looks creative but answers no question.
  • Name the problem before you celebrate the surface.

Source: course wording; Pass-1 discourse on originality theatre.

Ask: Which output this week was pretty but untethered to a question?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

4 · Assess judgment, not only surfaces

Studio assessment must see collaboration, reflection, and selection under AI — not only final pixels.

Image: Margaret Hamilton standing beside stacked Apollo software listings.

Margaret Hamilton - restoration · NASA / restored · Public domain · Source

  • Surfaces are easy to compare; judgment is harder and more important.
  • Portfolio traces make collaboration visible.
  • Aligns with course critical layer on GenAI authorship (C3).

Source: course wording; Park IASDR 2025 still candidate — do not cite until page-level citation resolve.

Ask: What evidence would prove you directed the tool?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

5 · Agency stays with the designer

Treat AI as collaborator or instrument — not as author of record.

Image: Block diagram of the Apollo Guidance Computer.

Apollo Guidance Computer block diagram · NASA · Public domain · Source

  • Tools can suggest; they do not carry professional responsibility.
  • Declare assistance; do not hide it behind polish.
  • Agency is practiced when you refuse an attractive wrong answer.

Source: course wording.

Ask: Where did you last override the model — and document it?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

6 · Name the costs

Critical reading of AI systems — power, labour, planet — belongs beside the toolkit.

Image: Ford assembly line workers in Copenhagen, 1923.

Ford assembly line in Copenhagen 1923 · Unknown · Public domain · Source

  • Every tool has upstream costs; design education should not pretend otherwise.
  • Optional deep cut: critical infrastructure literature (C1 adjacency).
  • Naming costs does not forbid tool use; it situates it.

Source: course wording; Crawford adjacency in professor brief only.

Ask: Which cost of your last GenAI session could you name in one sentence?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. In which studio stage does this unit place generative tools?
  2. What should a portfolio show besides the final image?
  3. What is originality theatre in one line?
  4. What should assessment see under AI, not only on screen?
  5. Who remains author of record?

Course geometric background · threshold · #7a624a21 · Original course SVG

  • Timer: 3 minutes. Students answer alone, from memory; then compare with a partner.
  • Practice only. Nothing is collected or graded.

Answers:

  • 1. Early variation / divergent opening — not final outsourcing (course wording).
  • 2. Prompts, edits, refusals, and selection decisions (process transparency).
  • 3. Pretty outputs without problem framing (originality theatre).
  • 4. Collaboration, reflection, and judgment — not only surfaces.
  • 5. The human designer (agency / authorship).

Ask: Which idea will you apply in the first Lab exercise?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

Exercise 1 · Question-led rough prototype (with or without GenAI)

Write one test question. Build only enough to answer it. Record every tool prompt and human edit.

The prototype is meant to answer questions, so keep it focused.

(Knapp, Zeratsky, and Kowitz 2016, chap. 13)

Save the brief, test question, before/after, prompts or manual steps, and the answer to the question.

Image: UNIVAC Unimatic computer terminal on display.

Univac Unimatic computer terminal at CHM · Unknown (CHM) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes (classroom adaptation of a 45-minute technique).
  • Use a shared class brief or your current D1 problem.
  • Write one question the prototype must answer; pick role, look and feel, or how it works.
  • If you use GenAI, stage it for variation only; you choose the final form.
  • Test with one classmate; record the answer.

Source: (Knapp, Zeratsky, and Kowitz 2016, chap. 13); GenAI staging is course wording.

Ask: What did the rough version teach that a polished render hid?

Creativity Techniques · U5 Creativity and Technology

Exercise 2 · Process trail

Lay out every version in order. Mark divergent and convergent moves. Name the turning point.

Save the ordered trail, diverge/converge marks, turning-point paragraph, and any tool prompts attached to each step.

Image: Historic photograph of a typewriter model.

Typewriter model LCCN2016821938 · Harris & Ewing · Public domain · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes.
  • Include sketches, exports, and discarded variants — not only the winner.
  • Mark where you opened options and where you closed them.
  • One paragraph: what changed your direction?

Source: classroom adaptation; catalogue witness urn:in-practice:exercise:a073813313fed5939b6194af (Creative Process Journals label). No single authoritative source quote — course wording.

Ask: Where would an assessor see your judgment in this trail?
